Effect of hydrogen bond donor on the choline chloride-based deep eutectic solvent-mediated extraction of lignin from pine wood

A R T I C L E I N F O Article history: Received 21 July 2020 Received in revised form 16 September 2020 Accepted 19 September 2020 Available online 28 September 2020 Keywords: Deep eutectic solvents Lignocellulose Solvatochromic parameters

ABSTRACT In this work, twenty-five kinds of choline chloride (ChCl)-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) containing acid, hydroxyl, amide, and binary hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) were prepared and successfully used to pretreat pine wood powder. As a result of the pretreatment, the glucan content in the pretreated biomass was increased, whereas the contents of hemicellulose and lignin were significantly decreased. The biomass pretreatment efficiency of the DESs had improved with increasing the polarity and hydrogen bond acidity (α) of the DESs. Among the studied DESs, ChCl:lactic acid:formic acid (1:1:1) with the highest α value was the most efficient DES in extracting lignin from biomass. The pretreated biomass also showed an enhanced enzymatic saccharification yield owing to the decreased particle size of the biomass and reduced content of hemicellulose and lignin. During the pretreatment process of biomass using DESs, the extracted lignin could be recovered successfully, with a yield of up to 60% and purity of over 90%. The molecular weight of the extracted lignin was much lower than that of the native cellulolytic enzyme lignin. The DES used for pretreatment process could be also successfully reused with high recovery yield of DES and high retention of delignification capacity. © 2020 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

## 1. Introduction Lignocellulosic biomass, such as agricultural residue, forestry waste, and waste paper, is a considerably abundant resource on earth and has long been considered as a potential sustainable source for biotransfor- mation into value-added bioproducts. However, the utility of lignocellu- losic biomass has been limited due to its recalcitrant structure [1-3]. The three primary biopolymers of lignocellulose are cellulose, hemicellu- lose, and lignin. Cellulose is highly crystalline, and the enzymatic hydro- lysis of cellulose is hindered by the existence of hemicellulose and lignin. Hemicellulose forms hydrogen bonds with cellulose and is cova- lently linked with lignin. Lignin is a highly branched aromatic polymer and acts as the glue that binds cellulose and hemicellulose in the ligno- cellulosic biomass. To improve the usability of lignocellulose by enhanc- ing the accessibility of enzymes, most pretreatment strategies have focused on removing the lignin from the lignocellulose and reducing the crystallinity [4]. Various pretreatment methods, such as steam or ammonia explosion, acid hydrolysis, alkaline hydrolysis, high- temperature organic solvent pretreatment, and enzymatic degradation, have been developed [5-7]. However, recent research has focused on the development of more energy-efficient and environmentally friendly

Recently, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been applied as green solvents for the pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass. DESs have emerged as alternatives to organic solvents and ionic liquids (ILs) owing to their nonvolatility, thermal stability, and nontoxicity. DESs can be prepared by simply mixing a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) with one or two hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and do not require purification [8–10]. Choline chloride (ChCl) is the most frequently used HBA in the preparation of DESs because of its inexpensive price, biocompatibility, and biodegradability [11]. Various HBDs, such as alcohols, amides, acids, and polyols, can be used to prepare the DESs. The properties of DESs can be easily controlled by changing the type and molar ratio of the HBA and HBD [12]. Therefore, biomass pretreatment processes using DESs have attracted attention in recent years. Alvarez-Vasco et al. reported that DESs are promising for the extraction of low molecular weight lignin from Douglas firs and poplar [13]. Xing et al. showed that dihydrogen-bonding DESs can be used as reaction media for the pretreatment of rice straw to enhance the fermentation yield [14]. Sai and Lee verified that ChCl:lactic acid is a promising pretreatment solvent for empty fruit bunches [15]. Liu et al. demonstrated that ChCl:lactic acid can efficiently delignify and produce nanocellulose from moso bamboo [16]. Liu et al. applied a microwave-assisted treatment using DESs to cleave the lignin-carbohydrate complex and extract lignin oligomers from poplar wood [1]. However, because the

physicochemical properties of DESs have not been clearly elucidated, previous studies have consisted primarily of arbitrarily screening suit- able DESs. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the physicochemical prop- erties of DESs and systematically analyze their effects during biomass pretreatment.

Solvatochromic parameters are especially useful to understand the physicochemical characteristics of solvents and are substantially corre-lated with various solvent properties such as extraction rate, chemical reaction rate, and solubility. These parameters can be easily measured using dyes with various UV-visible spectra depending on the nature of the solvent [17,18]. The most widely used solvatochromic parameters are the polarity scale (ET) and the Kamlet-Taft parameters, including dipolarity/polarizability (π*), hydrogen bond acidity (a), and hydrogen bond basicity (β). The betaine derivative ET (30), also known as Reichardt's dye, is the most widely used dye to determine the ET scale. However, because Reichardt's dye is sensitive to acid, dichloro-substituted betaine ET (33) and Nile red are more suitable for measuring the polarity of acidic solvents, such as DESs containing acid HBDs [19]. The solvatochromic parameters of green solvents, such as ionic liquid (ILs) and DESs, have been useful in understanding equilibrium and ki-netic phenomena recently [8,20,21]. For example, Doherty el al. re-ported that the solubility of biomass in ILs correlated well with the B values of the ILs [22].

In this study, twenty-five types of ChCl-based DESs containing one or two HBDs were prepared and used as pretreatment solvents for pine wood powder. The effects of HBDs on the pretreatment efficiency for such factors as the recovery of solid residue after treatment, hemicel- lulose removal, lignin removal, saccharification yield of the pretreated biomass, and recovery of the extracted lignin was investigated. Solvatochromic parameters, including polarity, dipolarity/polarizability, hydrogen bond acidity, and hydrogen bond basicity, were measured to understand the effects of HBDs on the DES properties. The correlation between the solvent properties and the pretreatment efficiency was also studied to explain the pretreatment mechanisms of the DESs on lig- nocellulosic biomass.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials N,N-Diethyl-4-nitroaniline (1) was provided by Frinton Laboratories Inc. (Hainesport, USA). Nile red (2), 4-nitroaniline (3), choline chloride (ChCl), urea (U), formamide (F), acetamide (A), glycerol (G), ethylene glycol (EG), diethylene glycol (DG), and triethylene glycol (TG) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, USA). Acetic acid (AA), citric acid (CA), formic acid (FA), lactic acid (LA), malic acid (MA), propionic acid (PA), succinic acid (SA), and xylitol (X) were supplied by Samchun Pure Chem. Co., Ltd. (Seoul, South Korea). Wood powder from *Pinus rigida* (average particle size: 141 µm) was purchased from G-Biotech (Seoul, South Korea). Celluclast® (63 FPU/mL, cellulase from *Trichoderma reesei*) was obtained from Novozymes (Bagsværd, Denmark). All other chemicals used in this study were of analytical grade and were used without further purification.

2.4. Compositional analysis of pretreated biomass The chemical composition of the pretreated wood powder and recovered lignin was analyzed according to the NREL method [24]. Briefly, the sample was treated with 72% (v/v) sulfuric acid at 30 °C for 2 h, followed by dilute acid (4%) at 121 °C for 1 h. The hydrolysis products (glucose, xylose, galactose, arabinose, and mannose) were determined using an HPLC (Young-Lin Model YL9100, South Korea) equipped with an RI detector and a Shodex SP0810 column operated at 85 °C. The mobile phase consisted of deionized water with a flow rate of 0.6 mL/min.

## 2.6. Enzymatic hydrolysis of pretreated biomass Enzymatic hydrolysis reactions were performed in 20 mL vials in a water bath at 120 rpm and 37 °C. Twenty milligrams of pretreated wood powder were subjected to cellulase hydrolysis for 24 h. The reaction was started by adding 16 µL Celluclast® to 1 mL of 50 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5.0) containing wood powder. After the saccharification period, the reaction mixtures were boiled for 3 min and centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 20 min to remove any unhydrolyzed substrate. The amount of reducing sugar released via enzymatic hydrolysis was measured using the dinitrosalicylic acid (DNS) method [25]. The reducing sugar yield was calculated using the following equation:
Reducing sugar yield (%) = Mass of released reducing sugar / Mass of glucose in the sample × 100(7)

The crystallinity index was determined via X-ray diffraction (XRD). The samples were scanned using a D8 ADVANCE Diffractometer (Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA) at 40 kV and 40 mA with 2-theta (θ) scan- ning from 2° to 40° at a 0.1° width. The FT-IR spectra of the samples were determined by an average of 16 scans per spectrum in the range 4000–600 cm⁻¹ (resolution of 4 cm⁻¹ and scanning interval of 1 cm⁻¹) using an FT/IR-4100 type A spectrometer (Jasco International Co. Ltd., Tokyo, Japan).

Molecular weight of recovered lignin The molecular weights of the lignin extracted with DES and cellulolytic enzyme lignin (CEL) were measured using an Agilent 1200S (Santa Clara, USA) with a multi-angle light scattering detector (miniDAWN TREOS). The column was operated at ambient temperatures and eluted at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. The Mn and Mw distributions were calibrated using polystyrene standards. Tetrahydrofuran (THF) was used as a mobile phase, and the lignin samples were acetylated in a pyridine and acetic anhydride mixture (1:1) prior to analysis.

CEL was prepared by following a previous procedure with slight modifications [27]. The wood powder was milled with a planetary ball mill (FRITSCH, Pulverisette 6, Germany) with a 500 mL sintered corundum bowl and 500 g sintered corundum balls (5 mm in diameter). The milling was performed at 500 rpm at room temperature for 24 h. The milled wood powder was then subjected to cellulase and hemicellulase hydrolysis (Novozyme 50199, Novozymes Korea, South Korea) for 24 h at 37 °C to remove the carbohydrates. The solid residue after enzymatic hydrolysis was washed with distilled water and then freeze-dried. The lignin was extracted from the freeze-dried sample using 95% dioxane for 24 h at ambient temperatures.

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass using DESs Twenty-five types of ChCl-based DESs containing acid, hydroxyl, amide, and binary HBDs were prepared and used to pretreat pine wood powder in this study (Table 1). All the prepared DESs could be used to extract glucan, hemicellulose, and lignin from pine wood powder. Table 2 shows the recovered weights and the chemical compositions of the solid residue after pretreating the wood powder using DESs. The recovered weights (%) after pretreatment using DESs with acid HBDs ranged from 47% to 71%, much lower than weights obtained after pretreatment using DESs with hydroxyl and amide HBDs. The recovered weights after pretreatment with DESs containing the binary (acid and hydroxyl) HBD were compared and linearly decreased with increasing the ratio of acid HBD. For example, the recovered weights for ChCl₁:LA₀:EG₂ (no. 9), ChCl₁:LA₀.₄:EG₁.₆ (no. 21), ChCl₁:LA₁.₂:EG₀.₈ (no. 25), and ChCl₁:LA₂:EG₀ (no. 4) were 95, 84, 67, and 55%, respectively. The DES-mediated pretreatment process extracted the hemicellulose and lignin more efficiently than extracting the glucan from wood powder. Therefore, the hemicellulose and lignin content in the

solid residue after DES pretreatment were lower than those in the un- treated wood powder, while the glucan contents in the solid residue were higher than those in the untreated wood powder. The ash content in the solid residue after DES pretreatment was about 30–70% of that in the untreated wood powder. Although the content of ash in the wood powder was quite small, the ash was also removed by the DES pretreat- ment process.

Fig. 1 shows the removal ratios of glucan, hemicellulose, and lignin from the wood powder pretreated with DESs. The DESs containing acid HBDs effectively extracted hemicellulose and lignin from the wood powder, with the removal ratios of hemicellulose ranging from 53% to 86%, much higher than the removal ratios obtained by DESs containing hydroxyl and amide HBDs (Fig. 1b). Among all the DESs tested, ChCl:FA was the most efficient DES to extract hemicellulose from the wood powder. The hemicellulose removal by DESs containing binary HBDs increased with the increase in the ratio of acid HBD. For example, hemicellulose removal for ChCl₁:PA₀:EG₂ (no. 9), ChCl₁:PA₀.₄:EG₁₆ (no. 20), ChCl₁:PA₁.₂:EG₀.₈ (no. 24), and ChCl₁:PA₂:EG₀ (no. 3) were 8, 9, 20, and 53%, respectively. The removal ratios of lignin from the wood powder by using DESs containing acid HBDs ranged from 41% to 70%, which is much higher than those obtained by DESs containing hydroxyl and amide HBDs (Fig. 1c). The ChCl:FA and ChCl:LA could efficiently extract lignin from the wood powder. For the DESs containing binary HBDs, the lignin removal increased with the increase in the ratio of acid HBD. For example, the lignin removal for ChCl₁:FA₀:EG₂ (no. 9), ChCl₁:FA₀.₄:EG₁₆ (no. 18), ChCl₁:FA₁.₂:EG₀.₈ (no. 22), and ChCl₁:FA₂:EG₀ (no. 1) were 14, 19, 52, and 70%, respectively. ChCl:LA:FA was the most efficient DES in extracting lignin, with 72% removal. Interestingly, the use of the binary HBDs LA:FA (1:1) could synergistically enhance the extraction capacity for lignin compared with ChCl:FA and ChCl:LA.

The removal ratio of hemicellulose correlated well with the that of lignin with a high correlation coefficient (R = 0.919, n = 25). This may indicate that the links between the hemicellulose and lignin were cleaved by the DES, and each compound had become dissolved in the DES. DESs are known to have a strong internal hydrogen bonding net- work, and, because of this property, the bonds between hemicellulose

and lignin can be broken [1]. The removal ratios of glucan from the wood powder using DESs containing acid HBDs ranged from 12% to 23%, which is higher than the removal ratios obtained by DESs contain- ing hydroxyl and amide HBDs (Fig. 1a). However, the removal ratio of glucan after DES pretreatment was much lower than those of hemicel- lulose and lignin. It is widely known that the solubility of cellulose in DES is extremely low [12,28]. Considering the results of previous stud- ies, it might be that glucose was mostly eluted from the hemicelluloses dissolved in the DES rather than cellulose. The high correlation coeffi- cient (R = 0.900, n = 25) between the hemicellulose removal and glu- can removal agrees with this conclusion. As a result of the DES- mediated pretreatment of pine wood powder, the glucan content in the pretreated solid residue increased regardless of the type of DES used. This result is due to the removal of significant amounts of hemicel- lulose and lignin in the pretreatment process using the DES.

3.2. Influence of DES characteristics on the pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass Understanding the solvent properties of DESs is helpful to explain their effects in the pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass. The solvatochromic parameters of the ChCl-based DESs with various HBDs were evaluated in this study (Table 3). The E_NR value quantifies the po- larity of a solvent using Nile red dye. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters are the most comprehensive and commonly used quantita- tive measurements of solvent properties [18,29]. Three solvatochromic parameters exist: π*, α, and β, which measure polarity/polarizability, hydrogen bond donating ability (acidity), and hydrogen bond accepting ability (basicity), respectively.

The E_NR values of the DESs in this study ranged from 47.6 to 50.9 and were lower than those of short-chain alcohols (the value for methanol is 52.0). These results indicate that the polarity of the DESs studied is higher than that of methanol and similar to that of water (E_NR = 48.2). The solvatochromic parameter π* represents the combination of the dipolarity and polarizability of the solvents. The π* values of the studied DESs ranged from 0.968 to 1.213 and were much higher than that of methanol (π* = 0.60). Most DESs exhibit similar π* values to dimethyl sulfoxide (π* = 1.00) and water (π* = 1.09). Among the DESs tested, ChCl:U exhibited the highest π* value, whereas ChCl: PA exhibited the lowest. The π* values of the ChCl-based DESs increased according to the HBD partner in the following order: PA < AA < TG < DG < MA < EG < FA < LA ≈ SA < CA < F < G < X < U.

The α value represents the hydrogen bond acidity normalized to a value of unity for methanol. The α values of the DESs examined covered a wide range from 0.606 to 1.344, ranging from that of *tert*-butanol (α = 0.68) through water (α = 1.17). Among the studied DESs, ChCl:LA:FA exhibited the highest α value, whereas ChCl:F exhibited the lowest α value. For the different HBD partners, the α values of the DESs increased in the following order: F < DG < EG < U < TG < X < G < PA < LA < SA < AA < MA < FA < CA.
The β value represents the solvent hydrogen bond basicity normal- ized to a value of unity for hexamethylphosphoramide. The β values of

the DESs studied in this work ranged from 0.387 to 0.684, or from the values for dioxane (β = 0.38) through N,N-dimethylformamide (β = 0.69). The DESs with a glycol HBD ex- hibited high β values, whereas the DESs with acid HBD exhibited poor ability to accept hydrogen bonds [18]. We also analyzed the relationship between the solvatochromic parameters of the DESs and their pretreatment efficiency for pine wood powder. When the four solvent parameters of all the studied DESs were correlated with the recovered weight of the solid residue after pretreatment, good correlations were obtained for the E_NR_ value (_R_ = 0.913, _n_ = 24) and hydrogen bond acidity (_R_ = 0.924, _n_ = 24). The recovered weight increased with an increase in the E_NR_ value, indicating that the high polarity of DESs is beneficial for extracting wood components from pine wood powder. 3.4. Influence of pretreatment temperature and time on biomass Considering the lignin removal ratio and enzymatic saccharification yield after pretreatment, ChCl:LA:FA was found to be the most effective DES for biomass pretreatment among the DESs studied. Therefore, ChCl: LA:FA was selected as the pretreatment solvent to identify the optimum pretreatment conditions. To find the optimum temperature for pre- treatment, wood powder was pretreated with the DES for 6 h at differ- ent temperatures ranging from 60 °C to 150 °C (Fig. 6a). When the temperature was increased from 60 °C to 80 °C, the lignin removal ratio did not increase significantly. However, the lignin removal in- creased sharply as the pretreatment temperature was increased from 80 °C to 100 °C and 130 °C. However, when the pretreatment tempera- ture was increased to 150 °C, no differences in the lignin removal ratio were observed compared with the biomass pretreated at 130 °C. The pretreatment time was varied between 1 and 12 h for analysis. In these experiments, the pretreatment temperature was fixed at 130 °C (Fig. 6b). The lignin removal ratio increased with increasing the pre- treatment time up to 6 h. However, after 6 h, the lignin removal ratio reached equilibrium. Overall, these results suggest that pretreatment at 130 °C for 6 h is optimal.

3.5. Recovery of extracted lignin After the DES-mediated pretreatment process to extract lignin, eth- anol was added to the treated wood to separate the solid residues from the DES. The DES–ethanol solution was separated via filtration, and the ethanol was removed using a rotary evaporator. The soluble fraction mostly contains hemicellulose, lignin, and DES. Lignin can be easily ob- tained from soluble fraction by precipitation using water as an anti- solvent at low temperature. The principle for the separation of hemicel- lulose and lignin is that the solubility of lignin decreases as the water content in the DES increases. The recovery yield and purity of lignin were measured when the pine wood powder was pretreated with acid DESs, which exhibited high lignin extraction efficiency (Fig. 7). The DESs that exhibited high lignin extraction efficiency were also effec- tive for recovering lignin from the DESs. The yields of lignin extracted with ChCl:FA, ChCl:LA, and ChCl:LA:FA were 61%, 53%, and 54%, respec- tively. Because the ChCl ions in the DESs bind to the phenol group of lig- nin, it is necessary to use a solvent that can effectively separate the lignin and DESs to increase the purity of the recovered lignin [38]. In this study, the lignin was washed with a water/ethanol (9:1, v/v) mix- ture, which has been reported to be effective for lignin and DES separa- tion [13]. The purity of the recovered lignin was not significantly affected by the type of HBD used and reached high values of 90–97%.

3.6. Recycling of DES used for biomass pretreatment The advantageous characteristics of DES distinguished from conven- tional solvents are low toxicity, nonvolatility, low cost, and recyclability. To develop the environmental-friendly biorefinery process using DES, the recyclability of DES should be considered. The ChCl:LA:FA, the most efficient DES to extract lignin from wood powder, was repeatedly used to investigate the efficiency of DES recovery and retainment of lig- nin extraction capacity (Fig. 9). The ChCl:LA:FA used for biomass pre- treatment could be recovered by evaporation of water due to the very low volatility and thermal stability of ChCl:LA:FA under 100 °C. ## 4. Conclusion Various ChCl-based DESs containing acid, hydroxyl, amide, and binary HBDs were prepared and successfully used to pretreat pine wood powder in this work. Among the studied DESs, those with acid HBDs were the most efficient to extract hemicellulose and lignin. As a result of the DES-mediated pretreatment of biomass, the resulting content of glucan increased, whereas the contents of hemicellulose and lignin were efficiently decreased. The correlation between the solvent properties of DESs and the pretreatment efficiency for biomass demonstrated that the polarity and hydrogen bond acidity of the DESs are the most important factor to extract hemicellulose and lignin from biomass. These results are meaningful to understand the extraction mechanism of hemicellulose and lignin from biomass by using DESs. In particular, ChCl:LA:FA, with the highest a value among the tested DESs, most efficiently extracted lignin from biomass. After pretreatment with DESs, the enzymatic saccharification yield of biomass was greatly enhanced. The increased reducing sugar yield could be explained by the decreased particle size and the reduced contents of hemicellulose and lignin in the biomass. During the pretreatment process of biomass using DESs, the extracted lignin could be recovered successfully with high yield and high purity. In addition, the DES used for pretreatment process could be also successfully reused with high recovery yield of DES and high retention of delignification capacity. Therefore, the results of this study will open up new opportunities for various applications of DESs for biomass pretreatment and lignin extraction.

As a result of the pretreatment, the glucan content in the pretreated biomass was increased, whereas the contents of hemicellulose and lignin were significantly decreased. The biomass pretreatment efficiency of the DESs had improved with increasing the polarity and hydrogen bond acidity (α) of the DESs. Among the studied DESs, ChCl:lactic acid:formic acid (1:1:1) with the highest α value was the most efficient DES in extracting lignin from biomass. The pretreated biomass also showed an enhanced enzymatic saccharification yield owing to the decreased particle size of the biomass and reduced content of hemicellulose and lignin. During the pretreatment process of biomass using DESs, the extracted lignin could be recovered successfully, with a yield of up to 60% and purity of over 90%. The molecular weight of the extracted lignin was much lower than that of the native cellulolytic enzyme lignin. The DES used for pretreatment process could be also successfully reused with high recovery yield of DES and high retention of delignification capacity. © 2020 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. ## 1. Introduction Lignocellulosic biomass, such as agricultural residue, forestry waste, and waste paper, is a considerably abundant resource on earth and has long been considered as a potential sustainable source for biotransfor- mation into value-added bioproducts. However, the utility of lignocellu- losic biomass has been limited due to its recalcitrant structure [1-3]. The three primary biopolymers of lignocellulose are cellulose, hemicellu- lose, and lignin. Cellulose is highly crystalline, and the enzymatic hydro- lysis of cellulose is hindered by the existence of hemicellulose and lignin. Hemicellulose forms hydrogen bonds with cellulose and is cova- lently linked with lignin. Lignin is a highly branched aromatic polymer and acts as the glue that binds cellulose and hemicellulose in the ligno- cellulosic biomass. To improve the usability of lignocellulose by enhanc- ing the accessibility of enzymes, most pretreatment strategies have focused on removing the lignin from the lignocellulose and reducing the crystallinity [4]. Various pretreatment methods, such as steam or ammonia explosion, acid hydrolysis, alkaline hydrolysis, high- temperature organic solvent pretreatment, and enzymatic degradation, have been developed [5-7]. However, recent research has focused on the development of more energy-efficient and environmentally friendly * --- Corresponding author. E-mail address: sanghlee@konkuk.ac.kr (S.H. Lee). 1 These authors contributed equally. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijbiomac.2020.09.145 0141-8130/© 2020 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. processes to selectively remove the lignin from lignocellulose and re- duce the degradation of cellulose. Recently, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been applied as green solvents for the pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass. DESs have emerged as alternatives to organic solvents and ionic liquids (ILs) owing to their nonvolatility, thermal stability, and nontoxicity. DESs can be prepared by simply mixing a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) with one or two hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and do not require purification [8–10]. Choline chloride (ChCl) is the most frequently used HBA in the preparation of DESs because of its inexpensive price, biocompatibility, and biodegradability [11]. Various HBDs, such as alcohols, amides, acids, and polyols, can be used to prepare the DESs. The properties of DESs can be easily controlled by changing the type and molar ratio of the HBA and HBD [12]. Therefore, biomass pretreatment processes using DESs have attracted attention in recent years. Alvarez-Vasco et al. reported that DESs are promising for the extraction of low molecular weight lignin from Douglas firs and poplar [13]. Xing et al. showed that dihydrogen-bonding DESs can be used as reaction media for the pretreatment of rice straw to enhance the fermentation yield [14]. Sai and Lee verified that ChCl:lactic acid is a promising pretreatment solvent for empty fruit bunches [15]. Liu et al. demonstrated that ChCl:lactic acid can efficiently delignify and produce nanocellulose from moso bamboo [16]. Liu et al. applied a microwave-assisted treatment using DESs to cleave the lignin-carbohydrate complex and extract lignin oligomers from poplar wood [1]. However, because the Y. Oh, S. Park, D. Jung et al. International Journal of Biological Macromolecules 165 (2020) 187–197 physicochemical properties of DESs have not been clearly elucidated, previous studies have consisted primarily of arbitrarily screening suit- able DESs. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the physicochemical prop- erties of DESs and systematically analyze their effects during biomass pretreatment. Solvatochromic parameters are especially useful to understand the physicochemical characteristics of solvents and are substantially corre-lated with various solvent properties such as extraction rate, chemical reaction rate, and solubility. These parameters can be easily measured using dyes with various UV-visible spectra depending on the nature of the solvent [17,18]. The most widely used solvatochromic parameters are the polarity scale (ET) and the Kamlet-Taft parameters, including dipolarity/polarizability (π*), hydrogen bond acidity (a), and hydrogen bond basicity (β). The betaine derivative ET (30), also known as Reichardt's dye, is the most widely used dye to determine the ET scale. However, because Reichardt's dye is sensitive to acid, dichloro-substituted betaine ET (33) and Nile red are more suitable for measuring the polarity of acidic solvents, such as DESs containing acid HBDs [19]. The solvatochromic parameters of green solvents, such as ionic liquid (ILs) and DESs, have been useful in understanding equilibrium and ki-netic phenomena recently [8,20,21]. For example, Doherty el al. re-ported that the solubility of biomass in ILs correlated well with the B values of the ILs [22]. In this study, twenty-five types of ChCl-based DESs containing one or two HBDs were prepared and used as pretreatment solvents for pine wood powder. The effects of HBDs on the pretreatment efficiency for such factors as the recovery of solid residue after treatment, hemicel- lulose removal, lignin removal, saccharification yield of the pretreated biomass, and recovery of the extracted lignin was investigated. Solvatochromic parameters, including polarity, dipolarity/polarizability, hydrogen bond acidity, and hydrogen bond basicity, were measured to understand the effects of HBDs on the DES properties. The correlation between the solvent properties and the pretreatment efficiency was also studied to explain the pretreatment mechanisms of the DESs on lig- nocellulosic biomass. ## 2. Therefore, ChCl: LA:FA was selected as the pretreatment solvent to identify the optimum pretreatment conditions. To find the optimum temperature for pre- treatment, wood powder was pretreated with the DES for 6 h at differ- ent temperatures ranging from 60 °C to 150 °C (Fig. 6a). Recovery of extracted lignin After the DES-mediated pretreatment process to extract lignin, eth- anol was added to the treated wood to separate the solid residues from the DES. The DES–ethanol solution was separated via filtration, and the ethanol was removed using a rotary evaporator. The soluble fraction mostly contains hemicellulose, lignin, and DES. Lignin can be easily ob- tained from soluble fraction by precipitation using water as an anti- solvent at low temperature. The principle for the separation of hemicel- lulose and lignin is that the solubility of lignin decreases as the water content in the DES increases. The recovery yield and purity of lignin were measured when the pine wood powder was pretreated with acid DESs, which exhibited high lignin extraction efficiency (Fig. 7). The DESs that exhibited high lignin extraction efficiency were also effec- tive for recovering lignin from the DESs. Conclusion Various ChCl-based DESs containing acid, hydroxyl, amide, and binary HBDs were prepared and successfully used to pretreat pine wood powder in this work. Among the studied DESs, those with acid HBDs were the most efficient to extract hemicellulose and lignin. As a result of the DES-mediated pretreatment of biomass, the resulting content of glucan increased, whereas the contents of hemicellulose and lignin were efficiently decreased. The correlation between the solvent properties of DESs and the pretreatment efficiency for biomass demonstrated that the polarity and hydrogen bond acidity of the DESs are the most important factor to extract hemicellulose and lignin from biomass. These results are meaningful to understand the extraction mechanism of hemicellulose and lignin from biomass by using DESs. In particular, ChCl:LA:FA, with the highest a value among the tested DESs, most efficiently extracted lignin from biomass. After pretreatment with DESs, the enzymatic saccharification yield of biomass was greatly enhanced. The increased reducing sugar yield could be explained by the decreased particle size and the reduced contents of hemicellulose and lignin in the biomass. During the pretreatment process of biomass using DESs, the extracted lignin could be recovered successfully with high yield and high purity. In addition, the DES used for pretreatment process could be also successfully reused with high recovery yield of DES and high retention of delignification capacity. Therefore, the results of this study will open up new opportunities for various applications of DESs for biomass pretreatment and lignin extraction. Hemicellulose forms hydrogen bonds with cellulose and is cova- lently linked with lignin. Lignin is a highly branched aromatic polymer and acts as the glue that binds cellulose and hemicellulose in the ligno- cellulosic biomass. Recently, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been applied as green solvents for the pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass. DESs have emerged as alternatives to organic solvents and ionic liquids (ILs) owing to their nonvolatility, thermal stability, and nontoxicity. Various HBDs, such as alcohols, amides, acids, and polyols, can be used to prepare the DESs. The properties of DESs can be easily controlled by changing the type and molar ratio of the HBA and HBD [12]. The most widely used solvatochromic parameters are the polarity scale (ET) and the Kamlet-Taft parameters, including dipolarity/polarizability (π*), hydrogen bond acidity (a), and hydrogen bond basicity (β). The betaine derivative ET (30), also known as Reichardt's dye, is the most widely used dye to determine the ET scale. However, because Reichardt's dye is sensitive to acid, dichloro-substituted betaine ET (33) and Nile red are more suitable for measuring the polarity of acidic solvents, such as DESs containing acid HBDs [19]. The solvatochromic parameters of green solvents, such as ionic liquid (ILs) and DESs, have been useful in understanding equilibrium and ki-netic phenomena recently [8,20,21]. For example, Doherty el al. re-ported that the solubility of biomass in ILs correlated well with the B values of the ILs [22]. In this study, twenty-five types of ChCl-based DESs containing one or two HBDs were prepared and used as pretreatment solvents for pine wood powder. The effects of HBDs on the pretreatment efficiency for such factors as the recovery of solid residue after treatment, hemicel- lulose removal, lignin removal, saccharification yield of the pretreated biomass, and recovery of the extracted lignin was investigated. Solvatochromic parameters, including polarity, dipolarity/polarizability, hydrogen bond acidity, and hydrogen bond basicity, were measured to understand the effects of HBDs on the DES properties. The correlation between the solvent properties and the pretreatment efficiency was also studied to explain the pretreatment mechanisms of the DESs on lig- nocellulosic biomass. ## 2. Influence of pretreatment temperature and time on biomass Considering the lignin removal ratio and enzymatic saccharification yield after pretreatment, ChCl:LA:FA was found to be the most effective DES for biomass pretreatment among the DESs studied. Therefore, ChCl: LA:FA was selected as the pretreatment solvent to identify the optimum pretreatment conditions. To find the optimum temperature for pre- treatment, wood powder was pretreated with the DES for 6 h at differ- ent temperatures ranging from 60 °C to 150 °C (Fig. 6a). When the temperature was increased from 60 °C to 80 °C, the lignin removal ratio did not increase significantly. However, the lignin removal in- creased sharply as the pretreatment temperature was increased from 80 °C to 100 °C and 130 °C. However, when the pretreatment tempera- ture was increased to 150 °C, no differences in the lignin removal ratio were observed compared with the biomass pretreated at 130 °C. The pretreatment time was varied between 1 and 12 h for analysis. In these experiments, the pretreatment temperature was fixed at 130 °C (Fig. 6b). The lignin removal ratio increased with increasing the pre- treatment time up to 6 h. However, after 6 h, the lignin removal ratio reached equilibrium. Overall, these results suggest that pretreatment at 130 °C for 6 h is optimal. 3.5. Recovery of extracted lignin After the DES-mediated pretreatment process to extract lignin, eth- anol was added to the treated wood to separate the solid residues from the DES. The DES–ethanol solution was separated via filtration, and the ethanol was removed using a rotary evaporator. The soluble fraction mostly contains hemicellulose, lignin, and DES. Lignin can be easily ob- tained from soluble fraction by precipitation using water as an anti- solvent at low temperature. The principle for the separation of hemicel- lulose and lignin is that the solubility of lignin decreases as the water content in the DES increases. The recovery yield and purity of lignin were measured when the pine wood powder was pretreated with acid DESs, which exhibited high lignin extraction efficiency (Fig. 7). The DESs that exhibited high lignin extraction efficiency were also effec- tive for recovering lignin from the DESs. The yields of lignin extracted with ChCl:FA, ChCl:LA, and ChCl:LA:FA were 61%, 53%, and 54%, respec- tively. In this study, the lignin was washed with a water/ethanol (9:1, v/v) mix- ture, which has been reported to be effective for lignin and DES separa- tion [13]. To develop the environmental-friendly biorefinery process using DES, the recyclability of DES should be considered. Conclusion Various ChCl-based DESs containing acid, hydroxyl, amide, and binary HBDs were prepared and successfully used to pretreat pine wood powder in this work. Among the studied DESs, those with acid HBDs were the most efficient to extract hemicellulose and lignin. As a result of the DES-mediated pretreatment of biomass, the resulting content of glucan increased, whereas the contents of hemicellulose and lignin were efficiently decreased. The correlation between the solvent properties of DESs and the pretreatment efficiency for biomass demonstrated that the polarity and hydrogen bond acidity of the DESs are the most important factor to extract hemicellulose and lignin from biomass. These results are meaningful to understand the extraction mechanism of hemicellulose and lignin from biomass by using DESs. In particular, ChCl:LA:FA, with the highest a value among the tested DESs, most efficiently extracted lignin from biomass. After pretreatment with DESs, the enzymatic saccharification yield of biomass was greatly enhanced. The increased reducing sugar yield could be explained by the decreased particle size and the reduced contents of hemicellulose and lignin in the biomass. During the pretreatment process of biomass using DESs, the extracted lignin could be recovered successfully with high yield and high purity. In addition, the DES used for pretreatment process could be also successfully reused with high recovery yield of DES and high retention of delignification capacity. Therefore, the results of this study will open up new opportunities for various applications of DESs for biomass pretreatment and lignin extraction.
